The top two differential diagnoses are endometrial hyperplasia (often estrogen-driven, possibly atypical or precancerous) and endometrial carcinoma — the latter being the most concerning and requiring urgent exclusion. Less common but important considerations include atrophic vaginitis, polyps, or less frequently, cervical or ovarian pathology. The single most discriminating initial test is transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) to measure endometrial thickness: an endometrial thickness ≤4 mm has a very high negative predictive value for endometrial cancer in postmenopausal women, while >4 mm warrants further investigation (e.g., endometrial biopsy). TVUS is noninvasive, widely available, and first-line per ACOG and ESHRE guidelines.
